core_summary: This chapter investigates recreational number theory, structural place value properties, digit frequency analysis, palindromic numbers, reverse-and-add algorithms, symmetric number grids, game theory winning strategies (the 21-game), and the Collatz Conjecture.
key_concepts: Digit Frequency Counting: Systematic analysis shows that across the range 1 to 100, each non-zero digit appears 20 times (10 times in the units place and 10 times in the tens place).
N-Digit Range Formula: The total count of N-digit numbers in base-10 place value is given by 9 x 10^(N-1).
Palindromic Numbers & Reverse-and-Add: Palindromes read identically forward and backward. Applying the Reverse-and-Add procedure iteratively transforms most starting integers into palindromes.
Collatz Conjecture Dynamics: Starting from any positive integer n, applying the rule f(n) = n/2 (if n is even) or f(n) = 3n + 1 (if n is odd) empirically always reaches the 4-2-1 loop.
Powers of 2 in Collatz Sequences: Any starting integer n = 2^k reaches 1 in exactly k halving steps.
Game of 21 Strategy: In a modulo-4 addition game to 21, Player 1 secures a guaranteed win by claiming target control numbers 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, and 21.

key_terms.definition: An integer that remains unchanged when its digits are written in reverse order (e.g., 121, 5775).
An unsolved problem in mathematics asserting that applying 3n+1 for odd numbers and n/2 for even numbers eventually reduces any positive integer to 1.
A procedure where a number is added to its digit-reversed partner repeatedly until a palindromic sum is obtained.
The numerical value of a digit determined by its positional column in base-10 notation.

key_takeaways: Systematic digit counting prevents common mistakes like undercounting double-digit occurrences like 77.
Game theory uses backward induction from target numbers to formulate winning strategies.
Simple deterministic rules like the Collatz rule can produce highly complex and unpredictable mathematical behavior.
